Integer-valued polynomials
satisfying growth constraintsThanks: The research of AN was supported in part by ISF Grant 3537/24.

Avner Kiro Address: A. Kiro, Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science, The Weizmann Institute of Science, 234 Herzl Street,Rehovot 76100, Israel Email address: avner-ephraiem.kiro@weizmann.ac.il and Alon Nishry Address: A. Nishry, School of Mathematical Sciences, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv 69978, Israel Email address: alonish@tauex.tau.ac.il
Abstract.

We consider polynomials which take integer values on the integers (IVPs), and satisfy an additional growth condition on the natural numbers. Elkies and Speyer, answering a question by Dimitrov, showed there is a critical exponential growth threshold, such that there are infinitely many IVPs with growth above the threshold and finitely many IVPs below that threshold (of arbitrary degree). In this paper, we give more refined estimates for the number of IVPs having exponential growth thresholds. In addition, we consider a similar problem, where there is a (not necessarily symmetric) growth condition on the integers. Notably, the critical threshold is determined by the logarithmic capacity of an explicit domain.

Key words and phrases: 
Integer-valued polynomials, Logarithmic capacity, Orthogonal polynomials, Moment matrices
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 30E05 . Secondary: 11C08 31A15 42C05

1. Introduction

Ruzsa’s conjecture asks whether a function f:ℕ→ℤf:{\mathbb{N}}\to{\mathbb{Z}} which satisfies

f⁡(m)−f⁡(n)≡0(modm−n)for all ​n,m∈ℕf(m)-f(n)\equiv 0\pmod{m-n}\quad\text{for all }n,m\in{\mathbb{N}}

and |f⁡(n)|<en|f(n)|<e^{n} for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} is a polynomial (see [Zan96]). Perhaps being motivated by this conjecture, Dimitrov [Dim13] asked if there are infinitely many integer-valued polynomials PP of arbitrary degree that satisfy

(1) |P⁡(n)|≤An​ for all ​n∈ℕ={0,1,2,…},|P(n)|\leq A^{n}\mbox{ for all }n\in{\mathbb{N}}=\{0,1,2,\dots\},

where A>1A>1 is fixed. Recall that an integer-valued polynomial (IVP) PP is an algebraic polynomial taking integer values on the natural numbers ℕ{\mathbb{N}} (or equivalently on the integers ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}). For more on IVPs see the book [CC97] and also the survey by Cahen and Chabert [CC16].

Elkies and Speyer [Dim13] proved that the threshold lies at the golden ratio, that is, if A<φ=12​(1+5)A<\varphi=\frac{1}{2}(1+\sqrt{5}) there are only finitely many such polynomials (of all degrees), while if A>φA>\varphi there are infinitely many of them. To the best of our knowledge the answer for A=φA=\varphi is still not known.

Our first theorem provide a small (asymptotic) improvement of the existence result.

Theorem 1.1.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there are infinitely many integer-valued polynomials PP that satisfy the inequalities

|P⁡(n)|≤(2​φ+ε)​φn,for all ​n∈ℕ.|P(n)|\leq\left(\sqrt{2\varphi}+\varepsilon\right)\varphi^{n},\quad\text{for all }n\in{\mathbb{N}}.
Remark.

We are not aware of any explicit example of an infinite family of IVPs satisfying the above inequalities (even after replacing the constant 2​φ\sqrt{2\varphi} by any larger absolute constant).

It is also possible to give ℓ2\ell^{2}-type results.

Theorem 1.2.

There are no (non-trivial) IVPs PP satisfying

∑n≥0|P⁡(n)|2​φ−2​n<φ.\sum_{n\geq 0}|P(n)|^{2}\varphi^{-2n}<\varphi.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, there are infinitely many IVPs PP that satisfy

∑n≥01n+1​|P⁡(n)|2​φ−2​n≤2π+ε.\sum_{n\geq 0}\tfrac{1}{n+1}|P(n)|^{2}\varphi^{-2n}\leq\frac{2}{\pi}+\varepsilon.
Remark.

Notice that for the constant IVP, P≡1P\equiv 1, it holds

∑n≥0φ−2​n=φ,\sum_{n\geq 0}\varphi^{-2n}=\varphi,

and moreover, taking P⁡(n)=12​n​(n+3)P(n)=\tfrac{1}{2}n(n+3), one can check that

∑n≥01n+1​|P⁡(n)|2​φ−2​n=4​φ2​log⁡(φ)−152​φ≊0.40<2π.\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{1}{n+1}|P(n)|^{2}\varphi^{-2n}=4\varphi^{2}\log(\varphi)-\frac{15}{2\varphi}\approxeq 0.40<\frac{2}{\pi}.

This bound can be improved, but we do not know the optimal bound (if one exists).

It is known [CC97, Chap. 1] that the sequence of binomial polynomials {(xk)}k∈ℕ\{\binom{x}{k}\}_{k\in{\mathbb{N}}} forms a basis over ℤ{\mathbb{Z}} for IVPs. That is, an IVP PP of degree at most dd can be written uniquely in the form

P⁡(x)=Pc​(x)=∑k=0dck​(xk),withc=(c0,…,cd)∈ℤd+1.P(x)=P_{\textbf{c}}(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_{k}\binom{x}{k},\quad\mbox{with}\quad\textbf{c}=(c_{0},\dots,c_{d})\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1}.

Hence, counting IVPs PP that satisfy the inequalities (1) is equivalent to counting integer lattice points inside the convex body

𝒞A​(d)={c=(c0,…,cd)∈ℝd+1:supn∈ℕ|Pc​(n)​A−n|≤1}.{\mathcal{C}}_{A}(d)=\left\{\textbf{c}=(c_{0},\dots,c_{d})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}\colon\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)A^{-n}|\leq 1\right\}.

It is well known that in order to bound the number of ℤd+1{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1} lattice points inside 𝒞A​(d){\mathcal{C}}_{A}(d) from below, it is sufficient to estimate Vol⁡(𝒞A​(d))\Vol\left({\mathcal{C}}_{A}(d)\right). On the other hand, to obtain an upper bound for the number of lattice points one has to use the special structure of this convex set.

Remark.

Note that since a polynomial of degree dd is determined by its values at (say) {0,…,d}\{0,\dots,d\}, there are finitely many polynomials of fixed degree dd that satisfy any of the inequalities in the theorems above.

2. The results

We are interested in estimating the number of IVPs of degree at most dd satisfying growth conditions on the integers such as (1) as the degree dd tends to infinity.

We begin by introducing some notation. Let A,B>1A,B>1 be fixed constants. We put c=c​(d)=(c0,…,cd)\textbf{c}=\textbf{c}(d)=(c_{0},\dots,c_{d}), and define the convex body

𝒞A,B∞(d;t)={c∈ℝd+1:supn∈ℕ|Pc(n)A−n|≤t,supn∈ℕ+|Pc(−n)B−n|≤t},{\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{\infty}(d;t)=\left\{\textbf{c}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}\colon\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)A^{-n}|\leq t,\>\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(-n)B^{-n}|\leq t\right\},

where ℕ={0,1,2,…},ℕ+={1,2,3,…}{\mathbb{N}}=\{0,1,2,\dots\},\,{\mathbb{N}}^{+}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}. Notice the ℤd+1{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1} lattice points in 𝒞A,B∞​(d,t){\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{\infty}(d;t) correspond to IVPs PP of degree at most dd satisfying the bounds

|P(n)|≤tAn,∀n∈ℕ,and|P(−n)|≤tBn,∀n∈ℕ+.|P(n)|\leq tA^{n},\quad\forall n\in{\mathbb{N}},\quad\text{and}\quad|P(-n)|\leq tB^{n},\quad\forall n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}.

Similarly, one may consider the ℓ2\ell^{2} bounds

∑n∈ℕ|P⁡(n)|2​A−2​n≤t2,and∑n∈ℕ+|P⁡(−n)|2​B−2​n≤t2,\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P(n)|^{2}A^{-2n}\leq t^{2},\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}}|P(-n)|^{2}B^{-2n}\leq t^{2},

corresponding to ℤd+1{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1} lattice points inside the set

𝒞A,B2(d;t)={c∈ℝd+1:∑n∈ℕ|Pc(n)|2A−2​n≤t2,∑n∈ℕ+|Pc(−n)|2B−2​n≤t2}.{\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{2}(d;t)=\left\{\textbf{c}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}\colon\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)|^{2}A^{-2n}\leq t^{2},\>\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(-n)|^{2}B^{-2n}\leq t^{2}\right\}.

It turns out that the volume of the convex bodies above is closely related to the logarithmic capacity of certain domains in the complex plane. The logarithmic capacity of a compact set E⊂ℂE\subset{\mathbb{C}} is given by (see [Ran95, Chap. 5])

Cap(E)≔exp(−infν∫E×Elog1|z−w|dν(z)dν(w)),\LCap\left({E}\right)\coloneqq\exp\left(-\inf_{\nu}\int_{E\times E}\log\frac{1}{|z-w|}\,\mathrm{d}\nu(z)\,\mathrm{d}\nu(w)\right),

where the infimum is taken over probability measures ν\nu supported on the set EE.

Put

𝔻1=𝔻⁡(1A2−1,AA2−1),𝔻2=𝔻⁡(B21−B2,BB2−1),{\mathbb{D}}_{1}={\mathbb{D}}\left({\frac{1}{A^{2}-1}},{\frac{A}{A^{2}-1}}\right),\>{\mathbb{D}}_{2}={\mathbb{D}}\left({\frac{B^{2}}{1-B^{2}}},{\frac{B}{B^{2}-1}}\right),

where 𝔻⁡(z,r){\mathbb{D}}(z,r) is the disk centered at zz and of radius rr. Notice that if A,B>1A,B>1, then 𝔻1∩𝔻2=∅{\mathbb{D}}_{1}\cap{\mathbb{D}}_{2}=\varnothing. See Figure 1.

It is known that the capacity of a disk is equal to its radius (e.g. [Ran95, Cor. 5.2.2]), e.g. Cap⁡(𝔻1)=AA2−1\LCap\left({{\mathbb{D}}_{1}}\right)=\frac{A}{A^{2}-1}. Note that the solution to the equation AA2−1=1\tfrac{A}{A^{2}-1}=1 with A>1A>1 is the golden ratio φ\varphi. This value of AA is the critical threshold for the volume of the set of polynomial coefficients 𝐜{\mathbf{c}}, for which the polynomial P𝐜P_{\mathbf{c}} satisfies the one-sided bound (1).

For the two-sided bounds, the following result gives the volume of the set of polynomial coefficients, and the asymptotic number of IVPs (depending on the degree) above the critical threshold.

Theorem 2.1.

Let A,B>1,t>1A,B>1,t>1 be fixed constants, 𝔻1,𝔻2{\mathbb{D}}_{1},{\mathbb{D}}_{2} as above, and

γA,B≔Cap⁡(𝔻1∪𝔻2).{\gamma}_{A,B}\coloneqq\LCap\left({{\mathbb{D}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{D}}_{2}}\right).

Then, as d→∞d\to\infty,

log⁡Vol⁡(𝒞A,B2​(d,t))\displaystyle\log\Vol\left({\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{2}(d;t)\right) =−12logγA,B⋅d2−12dlogd+O(dlogt),and\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}\log{\gamma}_{A,B}\cdot d^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}d\log d+O(d\log t),\quad\text{and}
log⁡Vol⁡(𝒞A,B∞​(d,t))\displaystyle\log\Vol\left({\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{\infty}(d;t)\right) =−12logγA,B⋅d2+O(dlogt).\displaystyle=-\tfrac{1}{2}\log{\gamma}_{A,B}\cdot d^{2}+O(d\log t).

Moreover, when γA,B∈(0,1){\gamma}_{A,B}\in(0,1) we have

log⁡#⁡{𝒞A,B2​(d,t)∩ℤd+1}=log⁡Vol⁡(𝒞A,B2​(d,t))+O⁡(d​log​t).\log\#\left\{{\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{2}(d;t)\cap{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1}\right\}=\log\Vol\left({\mathcal{C}}_{A,B}^{2}(d;t)\right)+O(d\log t).
Remark.

By the monotonicity of logarithmic capacity, we see that the region where γA,B∈(0,1)\gamma_{A,B}\in(0,1) is contained in the set A,B≥φA,B\geq\varphi.

Remark.

Using the Green function for an annulus (e.g. [CH53, V.15.7]) one can derive an expression for the capacity of the union of two disjoint disks in terms of theta functions. More precisely, one can show that

γA,B=12​exp⁡(log2⁡A+log2⁡B2​log⁡(A​B))​θ1′​(0,α)|θ1​(i​log⁡A,α)​θ1​(i​log⁡B,α)|,{\gamma}_{A,B}=\tfrac{1}{2}\exp\left(\frac{\log^{2}A+\log^{2}B}{2\log(AB)}\right)\frac{\theta_{1}^{\prime}(0,{\alpha})}{\sqrt{|\theta_{1}(i\log A,{\alpha})\theta_{1}(i\log B,{\alpha})|}},

where α=(A​B)−1{\alpha}=(AB)^{-1}, θ1\theta_{1} is a theta function (see e.g. [AS92, 16.27 f.]). Here we used a modification of a formula due to Ransford, see [LSN17, Example 4.7].

See Figure 2 for an illustration of the level sets of γA,B\gamma_{A,B} using Mathematica. The dashed line corresponds to the critical level set γA,B=1\gamma_{A,B}=1.

At the critical threshold, we can prove the analogs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, up to the calculation of the explicit constants (which depend on A,BA,B).

Theorem 2.2.

Let A,B>1A,B>1 be fixed constants as in Theorem 2.1 that satisfy γA,B=1\gamma_{A,B}=1. There is a constant C1=C1​(A,B)>0C_{1}=C_{1}(A,B)>0 so that there are infinitely many IVPs PP satisying

|Pc​(n)|≤C1​An,for all ​n∈ℕ​ and ​|Pc​(−n)|≤C1​Bn,for all ​n∈ℕ+.|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)|\leq C_{1}A^{n},\>\>\text{for all }n\in{\mathbb{N}}\text{ and }|P_{\textbf{c}}(-n)|\leq C_{1}B^{n},\>\>\text{for all }n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}.
Theorem 2.3.

Let A,B>1A,B>1 be fixed constants as in Theorem 2.1 that satisfy γA,B=1\gamma_{A,B}=1. There is a constant C2=C2​(A,B)>0C_{2}=C_{2}(A,B)>0 so that there are no IVPs PP that satisfy

∑n∈ℕ|Pc​(n)|2​A−2​n≤C2, and ​∑n∈ℕ+|Pc​(−n)|2​B−2​n≤C2.\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)|^{2}A^{-2n}\leq C_{2},\text{ and }\>\>\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(-n)|^{2}B^{-2n}\leq C_{2}.

Moreover, there is a constant C3=C3​(A,B)>0C_{3}=C_{3}(A,B)>0, such that there are infinitely many IVPs PP satsifying

∑n∈ℕ|Pc​(n)|2n+1​A−2​n≤C3, and ​∑n∈ℕ+|Pc​(−n)|2n+1​B−2​n≤C3.\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\frac{|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)|^{2}}{n+1}A^{-2n}\leq C_{3},\text{ and }\>\>\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}}\frac{|P_{\textbf{c}}(-n)|^{2}}{n+1}B^{-2n}\leq C_{3}.

Notation

We will use the following notation for the disk and the circle. 𝔻⁡(a,r)={z∈ℂ:|z−a|<r}{\mathbb{D}}(a,r)=\{z\in{\mathbb{C}}\colon|z-a|<r\}, 𝕋⁡(a,r)=∂𝔻⁡(a,r){\mathbb{T}}(a,r)=\partial{\mathbb{D}}(a,r). We also write 𝔻=𝔻⁡(0,1){\mathbb{D}}={\mathbb{D}}(0,1), 𝕋=∂𝔻{\mathbb{T}}=\partial{\mathbb{D}} for the unit disk and unit circle.

We write d​|z|\mathrm{d}|z| to denote integration with respect to arc-length measure, and d​A​(z)\mathrm{d}A(z) denotes integration with respect to area measure (both are not normalized). That is, if Γ{\Gamma} is a (rectifiable) curve, and GG is a domain, then

∫Γ1​d​|z|=length​(Γ),∫G1​𝑑A​(z)=area​(G).\int_{\Gamma}1\,\mathrm{d}|z|=\textrm{length}({\Gamma}),\qquad\int_{G}1\,\mathrm{d}A(z)=\textrm{area}(G).

3. Outline of the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2

Here we give a summary of the ideas behind the proofs of the theorems with a growth condition on the natural numbers. Using the binomial polynomial basis

(zk)=z⁡(z−1)​…​(z−k+1)k!,k∈ℕ,\binom{z}{k}=\frac{z(z-1)\dots(z-k+1)}{k!},\quad k\in{\mathbb{N}},

we let

P⁡(z)=P𝐜​(z)=∑k=0dck​(zk)P(z)=P_{\bf c}(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_{k}\binom{z}{k}

be a polynomial of degree dd. The polynomial P𝐜P_{\bf c} is integer-valued if and only if 𝐜=(c0,…,cd)∈ℤd+1{\bf c}=(c_{0},\dots,c_{d})\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1}. The key observation is that the generating function

gP​(z)≔∑n∈ℕP⁡(n)​zn=11−z​∑k=0dck​(z1−z)k,∀|z|<1,g_{P}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}P(n)z^{n}=\frac{1}{1-z}\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_{k}\left(\frac{z}{1-z}\right)^{k},\qquad\forall|z|<1,

can be utilized to obtain information on c given the sequence {P⁡(n)}n∈ℕ\{P(n)\}_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} and vice versa.

3.1. The ℓ∞\ell^{\infty} constraint

Let t>0t>0. We first consider the (easier) problem of the asymptotic volume of the set

{c∈ℝd+1:supn∈ℕ|Pc​(n)​A−n|≤t}.\left\{\textbf{c}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}\colon\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P_{\textbf{c}}(n)A^{-n}|\leq t\right\}.

Using theorems by Ball and Vaaler, and some approximations (see Section 4 for the details), we will arrive at the following result

td+1detℳ≤Vol⁡({c∈ℝd+1:supn∈ℕ|P𝐜​(n)​rn|≤12​t})≤C1d+1​td+1detℳ,\frac{t^{d+1}}{\sqrt{\det{\mathcal{M}}}}\leq\Vol\left(\Big\{\textbf{c}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}\colon\sup_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|P_{\bf c}(n)r^{n}|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}t\Big\}\right)\leq\frac{C_{1}^{d+1}t^{d+1}}{\sqrt{\det{\mathcal{M}}}},

where C1>0C_{1}>0 is an absolute constant, and

ℳ=ℳ⁡(d,r)=[∑n=0∞(nj)​(nk)​r2​n]j,k=0d.{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{M}}(d;r)=\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{k}r^{2n}\right]_{j,k=0}^{d}.

Observe that by the orthogonality of the monomials

∑n=0∞P1​(n)​P2​(n)​r2​n\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_{1}(n)P_{2}(n)r^{2n} =12​π​r​∫r​𝕋[∑m=0∞P1​(m)​wm]​[∑n=0∞P2​(n)​w¯n]​d​|w|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{r{\mathbb{T}}}\left[\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}P_{1}(m)w^{m}\right]\left[\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_{2}(n)\bar{w}^{n}\right]\mathrm{d}|w|
=12​π​r​∫r​𝕋gP1​(w)​gP2​(w)¯​d​|w|,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{r{\mathbb{T}}}g_{P_{1}}(w)\overline{g_{P_{2}}(w)}\,\mathrm{d}|w|,

where the integrals are with respect to arc-length.

By a change of variables, using the fractional linear transformation w=z/(1−z)w=z/(1-z), we conclude that

ℳ=[12​π​r​∫𝕋1wj​w¯k​d​|w|]j,k=0d{\mathcal{M}}=\left[\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}w^{j}\bar{w}^{k}\,\mathrm{d}|w|\right]_{j,k=0}^{d}

is a moment matrix, where

𝔻1=𝔻⁡(r21−r2,r1−r2),𝕋1=∂𝔻1=𝕋⁡(r21−r2,r1−r2).{\mathbb{D}}_{1}={\mathbb{D}}\left(\frac{r^{2}}{1-r^{2}},\frac{r}{1-r^{2}}\right),\quad{\mathbb{T}}_{1}=\partial{\mathbb{D}}_{1}={\mathbb{T}}\left(\frac{r^{2}}{1-r^{2}},\frac{r}{1-r^{2}}\right).

It is known that (see e.g. Appendix A)

detℳ=∏k=0d‖qk‖L2​(μ)2,\det{\mathcal{M}}=\prod_{k=0}^{d}\|q_{k}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu)},

where qkq_{k} is the monic orthogonal polynomial (of degree kk) with respect to μ\mu – the arc-length measure on 𝕋1{\mathbb{T}}_{1} (weighted by 12​π​r\frac{1}{2\pi r}). These polynomials and their norms are given explicitly by

qk​(w)=(w−r21−r2)k,‖qk‖L2​(μ)2=1r​(r1−r2)2​k+1,q_{k}(w)=\big(w-\tfrac{r^{2}}{1-r^{2}}\big)^{k},\qquad\|q_{k}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu)}=\frac{1}{r}\Big(\frac{r}{1-r^{2}}\Big)^{2k+1},

detℳ=1rd+1​(r1−r2)(d+1)2.\det{\mathcal{M}}=\frac{1}{r^{d+1}}\Big(\frac{r}{1-r^{2}}\Big)^{(d+1)^{2}}.

The critical threshold is achieved when r1−r2=1\frac{r}{1-r^{2}}=1, that is r=φ−1r=\varphi^{-1}. Theorem 1.1 which concerns lattice points is obtained using a related theorem of Vaaler.

3.2. The ℓ2\ell^{2} constraint

Here we have, for r<1r<1,

12​π​r​∫r​𝕋|gP​(z)|2​d​|z|=∑n=0∞|P⁡(n)|2​r2​n=‖an‖ℓ22,\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{r{\mathbb{T}}}|g_{P}(z)|^{2}\mathrm{d}|z|=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|P(n)|^{2}r^{2n}=\|a_{n}\|^{2}_{\ell^{2}},

Again making the change of variables w=z/(1−z)w=z/(1-z), we find that

‖an‖ℓ22=12​π​r​∫𝕋1|hc​(w)|2​d​|w|,‖ann+1‖ℓ22=1π​r2​∫𝔻1|hc​(w)|2​d​A​(w)|1+w|2,\|a_{n}\|^{2}_{\ell^{2}}=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{{\mathbb{T}}_{1}}|h_{\textbf{c}}(w)|^{2}\mathrm{d}|w|,\qquad\Big\|\frac{a_{n}}{\sqrt{n+1}}\Big\|^{2}_{\ell^{2}}=\frac{1}{\pi r^{2}}\int_{{\mathbb{D}}_{1}}|h_{\textbf{c}}(w)|^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}A(w)}{|1+w|^{2}},

where 𝔻1{\mathbb{D}}_{1} and 𝕋1{\mathbb{T}}_{1} are as above, and

h𝐜​(w)=∑k=0dck​wk.h_{\bf c}(w)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}c_{k}w^{k}.

Let qkq_{k} be the (Szegő) monic orthogonal polynomial with respect to the measure μ\mu as above, and tkt_{k} be the (Bergman) monic orthogonal polynomial, with respect to weighted area measure

d​ν​(w)=d​A​(w)π​r2​|1+w|2on𝔻1.\mathrm{d}\nu(w)=\frac{\mathrm{d}A(w)}{\pi r^{2}|1+w|^{2}}\quad\text{on}\quad{\mathbb{D}}_{1}.

We are not aware of any simple formula for the tkt_{k}s (see e.g. [Gus+09, Remark 8.1]). However, by results of Korovkin (see Section 5.1) we have, with r=φ−1r=\varphi^{-1}, and some q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1),

‖tk‖L2​(ν)2=1k+1+O⁡(qk).\|t_{k}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\nu)}=\frac{1}{k+1}+O(q^{k}).

We obtain the correspondences

∑n=0∞|P𝐜​(n)|2​φ−2​n≤t2⇔∑k=0d|αk​(𝐜)|2​‖qk‖L2​(μ)2=φ​∑k=0d|αk​(𝐜)|2≤t2,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|P_{\bf c}(n)|^{2}\varphi^{-2n}\leq t^{2}\iff\sum_{k=0}^{d}|\alpha_{k}({\bf c})|^{2}\|q_{k}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu)}=\varphi\sum_{k=0}^{d}|\alpha_{k}({\bf c})|^{2}\leq t^{2},

where h𝐜=∑k=0dαk​(𝐜)​qkh_{\bf c}=\sum_{k=0}^{d}\alpha_{k}({\bf c})q_{k}, and

∑n=0∞|P⁡(n)|2n+1​φ−2​n≤t2⇔∑k=0d|βk​(𝐜)|2​‖tk‖L2​(ν)2≤t2,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{|P(n)|^{2}}{n+1}\varphi^{-2n}\leq t^{2}\iff\sum_{k=0}^{d}|\beta_{k}({\bf c})|^{2}\|t_{k}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\nu)}\leq t^{2},

where now h𝐜=∑k=0dβk​(𝐜)​tkh_{\bf c}=\sum_{k=0}^{d}\beta_{k}({\bf c})t_{k}. The proof of the first part of Theorem 1.2 follows by observing that since qkq_{k} are monic polynomials, if h𝐜h_{\bf c} has integer coefficients, then the first, in decreasing order of kk, non-zero coefficient αk​(𝐜)\alpha_{k}({\bf c}) is the same integer. The second part of the theorem is deduced from a classical theorem of van der Corput on the existence of lattice points inside symmetric convex bodies with a large volume.

4. Preliminaries

4.1. Generating functions

To an algebraic polynomial PP we associate the generating function

(2) g⁡(z)=gP​(z)=∑n=0∞P⁡(n)​zn,g(z)=g_{P}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P(n)z^{n},

which converges for |z|<1|z|<1. We also denote by gkg_{k} the generating function of the binomial polynomial (⋅k)\binom{\cdot}{k}. We leave the proof of the following claim as an exercise to the reader.

Claim 4.1.

For |z|<1|z|<1 and k≥0k\geq 0, we have

gk​(z)=11−z​(z1−z)k.g_{k}(z)=\frac{1}{1-z}\left(\frac{z}{1-z}\right)^{k}.

The above claim provides an analytic continuation of gPg_{P} to a meromorphic function.

Claim 4.2.

For any polynomial PP, the function gPg_{P} is analytic in ℂ∖{1}{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{1\} with g⁡(∞)=0g(\infty)=0, and in addition

(3) gP(z)=−∑n=1∞P⁡(−n)znfor all |z|>1.g_{P}(z)=-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{P(-n)}{z^{n}}\quad\mbox{for all }|z|>1.

For a more general claim see [Levin, Lecture 1010, Remark 11].

Any polynomial PP of degree dd can be written in a unique way as

hence it is sufficient to prove the claim for binomials. By Claim 4.1, for k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} we have that

gk​(z)=∑n∈ℕ(nk)​zn=zk(1−z)k+1,|z|<1,g_{k}(z)=\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}\binom{n}{k}z^{n}=\frac{z^{k}}{(1-z)^{k+1}},\qquad|z|<1,

where the right hand side is analytic in z∈ℂ∖{1}z\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus\{1\} and vanishes at infinity. Let ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). Using the vanishing of gkg_{k} at infinity, and Cauchy’s integral formula, we have

(nk)=12​π​i∫|w|=εwk(1−w)k+1d​wwn+1=−12​π​i∫|w−1|=εwk(1−w)k+1d​wwn+1.\binom{n}{k}=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{|w|=\varepsilon}\frac{w^{k}}{(1-w)^{k+1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}w}{w^{n+1}}=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{|w-1|=\varepsilon}\frac{w^{k}}{(1-w)^{k+1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}w}{w^{n+1}}.

We will use wz=exp⁡(z​log⁡w)w^{z}=\exp(z\log w), where the principal branch of log\log, cut along the ray (−∞,0](-\infty,0] is chosen. Observe that with this choice,

Q(z)≔−12​π​i∫|w−1|=εwk(1−w)k+1d​wwz+1,Q(z)\coloneqq-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{|w-1|=\varepsilon}\frac{w^{k}}{(1-w)^{k+1}}\frac{\mathrm{d}w}{w^{z+1}},

Since the polynomials QQ and (⋅k)\binom{\cdot}{k} coincide on the (infinite) set ℕ{\mathbb{N}}, we conclude they are equal. In particular, for n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}},

By making a change of variables ζ=1/w\zeta=1/w, so that dw/w=−dζ/ζ\mathrm{d}w/w=-\mathrm{d}\zeta/\zeta, and shifting the contour we find

4.2. Tools for the ℓ∞\ell^{\infty} case

Let N,k∈ℕN,k\in{\mathbb{N}} with N>kN>k, and let Σ\Sigma be an N×kN\times k matrix of maximal rank kk. We use the following version of a result by Vaaler [Vaa79, Thms. 1 and 2], see also Gluskin-Kashin [GK92].

Theorem 4.5.

We have that

VN≔Vol⁡({c=(c1,…,ck)∈ℝk:supn≤N|∑j=1kcj​Σn,j|≤12})≥1detΣt​Σ.V_{N}\coloneqq\Vol\left(\Big\{\textbf{c}=(c_{1},\dots,c_{k})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\colon\sup_{n\leq N}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}\Sigma_{n,j}\Big|\leq\tfrac{1}{2}\Big\}\right)\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{\det\Sigma^{t}\Sigma}}.

Moreover, if R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} is such that

R2⋅detΣt​Σ≤1,R^{2}\cdot\det\Sigma^{t}\Sigma\leq 1,

then there are at least 2​R2R non-trivial integer solutions c∈ℤk\textbf{c}\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{k} to the system of inequalities

|∑j=1kcj​Σn,j|≤1for alln∈{1,…,N}.\left|\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}\Sigma_{n,j}\right|\leq 1\qquad\mbox{for all}\quad n\in\{1,\dots,N\}.

In the other direction we use a result of Ball [Bal89] (also Gluskin-Kashin [GK92]).

Theorem 4.6.

We have that

Vol⁡({c=(c1,…,ck)∈ℝk:supn≤N|∑j=1kcj​Σn,j|≤1})≤2N−kdetΣt​Σ.\Vol\left(\Big\{\textbf{c}=(c_{1},\dots,c_{k})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{k}\colon\sup_{n\leq N}\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{k}c_{j}\Sigma_{n,j}\Big|\leq 1\Big\}\right)\leq\frac{\sqrt{2}^{N-k}}{\sqrt{\det\Sigma^{t}\Sigma}}.

For the convenience of the reader we prove the following standard result in Appendix A.

Theorem 4.7.

Let μ\mu be a measure on ℂ{\mathbb{C}} with infinite support and finite moments of all orders. Define the nn-th moment matrix by

ℳ⁡(n,μ)=[Mk,m]k,m=0n,Mk,m=∫ℂzj​z¯k​𝑑μ​(z).{\mathcal{M}}(n;\mu)=\left[M_{k,m}\right]_{k,m=0}^{n},\qquad M_{k,m}=\int_{\mathbb{C}}z^{j}\bar{z}^{k}\,\mathrm{d}\mu(z).

Then

detℳ⁡(n,μ)=∏j=0n‖Qj‖L2​(μ)2,\det{\mathcal{M}}(n;\mu)=\prod_{j=0}^{n}\left\|Q_{j}\right\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\mu)},

where QjQ_{j} are the orthogonal monic polynomials, with respect to μ\mu.

Let η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). Suppose Γ=𝕋1∪𝕋2{\Gamma}={\mathbb{T}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{T}}_{2} is the union of two circles with disjoint interiors, whose radii are bounded between η\eta and 1η\frac{1}{\eta}, and are separated by at least η\eta and at most 1η\frac{1}{\eta}. Denote the n×nn\times n moment matrix, with respect to arc-length measure on Γ{\Gamma}, by ℳΓ​(n){\mathcal{M}}_{{\Gamma}}(n). We will need an effective lower bound for the smallest eigenvalue of ℳΓ​(n){\mathcal{M}}_{{\Gamma}}(n), which is given by

λn−1=max{12​π∫−ππ|P(ei​θ)|2dθ:degP=n,∫Γ|P(z)|2|dz|=1}.\lambda_{n}^{-1}=\max\left\{\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\left|P(e^{i\theta})\right|^{2}\mathrm{d}\theta\,\colon\,\deg P=n,\,\,\int_{\Gamma}|P(z)|^{2}|\mathrm{d}z|=1\right\}.

The following result is obtained by combining [Wid69, Theorem 7.3 and Eq. (10.5)].

Proposition 4.8.

Using the same notation as above, and under the same assumptions, we have

λn≥exp⁡(−CΓ​n),\lambda_{n}\geq\exp(-C_{{\Gamma}}n),

where the constant CΓ>0C_{{\Gamma}}>0 depends continuously on the Green function of the exterior of Γ{\Gamma} (and its derivatives).

Under the assumptions above the constant CΓC_{{\Gamma}} can be bounded in terms of η\eta only.

Lemma 4.10.

4.3. Tools for the ℓ2\ell^{2} case

Below we will need an estimate for the number of lattice points inside ellipsoids of a special type.

Proposition 4.17.

Let d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} and γ,t>0\gamma,t>0 be parameters (that may depend on dd), and define the ellipsoid

ℰ=ℰ⁡(d,γ,t)={x=(x0,…,xd)∈ℝd+1:∑k=0dxk2​γ2​k≤t2}.{\mathcal{E}}={\mathcal{E}}(d;\gamma,t)=\left\{\textbf{x}=(x_{0},\dots,x_{d})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d+1}\colon\sum_{k=0}^{d}x_{k}^{2}\gamma^{2k}\leq t^{2}\right\}.

Moreover, let Ψ\Psi be a lower unipotent matrix, that is, an n×nn\times n lower triangular matrix, with diagonal elements all equal to 11. We denote by Ψ⁡(ℰ)\Psi({\mathcal{E}}) the image of ℰ{\mathcal{E}} under Ψ\Psi. Note that this map preserves volume.

For γ≤1≤t\gamma\leq 1\leq t we have

−C1​(d+1)≤log⁡#⁡(Ψ⁡(ℰ)∩ℤd+1)Vol⁡(ℰ)≤C2​(d+1)​log⁡min⁡{d+1,(1−γ)−1},-C_{1}(d+1)\leq\log\frac{\#\left(\Psi({\mathcal{E}})\cap{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1}\right)}{\Vol\left({\mathcal{E}}\right)}\leq C_{2}(d+1)\log\min\{d+1,(1-\gamma)^{-1}\},

where C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 are absolute constants.

Remark.

Notice that Vol(ℰ)=γ−d(d+1)/2td+1Vol(B2d+1)\Vol\left({\mathcal{E}}\right)=\gamma^{-d(d+1)/2}t^{d+1}\Vol\left(B_{2}^{d+1}\right).

Proof.

The lower bound (with C1=log⁡2C_{1}=\log 2) follows from [GL87, Sec. 7, Thm. 4].

Let 𝐳1,𝐳2∈Ψ⁡(ℰ)∩ℤd+1\mathbf{z}_{1},\mathbf{z}_{2}\in\Psi({\mathcal{E}})\cap{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1} be two different lattice points. Notice that by the structure of the matrix Ψ\Psi, we have that

‖𝐱1−𝐱2‖∞≔‖Ψ−1​(𝐳1)−Ψ−1​(𝐳2)‖∞≥1.\|\mathbf{x}_{1}-\mathbf{x}_{2}\|_{\infty}\coloneqq\|\Psi^{-1}(\mathbf{z}_{1})-\Psi^{-1}(\mathbf{z}_{2})\|_{\infty}\geq 1.

Now let 𝐱=(x0,…,xd)∈ℰ\mathbf{x}=(x_{0},\dots,x_{d})\in{\mathcal{E}} be one of the preimages of a ℤd+1{\mathbb{Z}}^{d+1} lattice point in Ψ⁡(ℰ)\Psi({\mathcal{E}}). If 𝐲=(y0,…,yd)∈[−12,12]d+1\mathbf{y}=(y_{0},\dots,y_{d})\in\left[-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\right]^{d+1}, then

∑k=0d(xk+yk)2​γ2​k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{d}(x_{k}+y_{k})^{2}\gamma^{2k} =∑k=0dxk2​γ2​k+2​∑k=0dxk​yk​γ2​k+∑k=0dyk2​γ2​k\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{d}x_{k}^{2}\gamma^{2k}+2\sum_{k=0}^{d}x_{k}y_{k}\gamma^{2k}+\sum_{k=0}^{d}y_{k}^{2}\gamma^{2k}
≤2​[t2+14​min⁡{d+1,(1−γ2)−1}],\displaystyle\leq 2\left[t^{2}+\tfrac{1}{4}\min\{d+1,(1-\gamma^{2})^{-1}\}\right],

since 2​|xk​yk|≤xk2+yk22|x_{k}y_{k}|\leq x_{k}^{2}+y_{k}^{2}. Therefore, if we denote by 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} the union of all the cubes with side length 11 centered at preimages of lattice points inside ℰ{\mathcal{E}}, we see that

𝒬⊂C2​(1+t−2​min⁡{d+1,(1−γ)−1}​ℰ⊂C2​min⁡{d+1,(1−γ)−1}​ℰCLOSE.{\mathcal{Q}}\subset C_{2}(1+t^{-2}\min\{d+1,(1-\gamma)^{-1}\}{\mathcal{E}}\subset C_{2}\min\{d+1,(1-\gamma)^{-1}\}{\mathcal{E}}.

Since the cubes forming 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} are of volume 11 and have disjoint interiors we get the required bound for the number of lattice points. ∎

The following theorem can be proved explicitly using conformal maps, but it also follows as a very special case of [Wid69, Thm. 9.1]. The fine properties of the normalizing constants can be found in [Wid69, Sec. 6].

Let η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). Suppose Γ=𝕋1∪𝕋2{\Gamma}={\mathbb{T}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{T}}_{2} is the union of two circles with disjoint interiors, whose radii are bounded between η\eta and 1η\frac{1}{\eta}, and are separated by at least η\eta and at most 1η\frac{1}{\eta}. Appendix B Bergman polynomials on two disks

Here we proved Theorem 4.19. We use the method of the paper [Gus+09] (simplified for a domain which is the union of two disks).

Let η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), G=𝔻1∪𝔻2G={\mathbb{D}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{D}}_{2} be the disjoint union of two disks, whose radii are bounded between η\eta and 1η\frac{1}{\eta}, and are separated by at least η\eta and at most 1η\frac{1}{\eta}. Put Γ=∂G=𝕋1∪𝕋2\Gamma=\partial G={\mathbb{T}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{T}}_{2}.

We denote by {tn}n=0∞\{t_{n}\}_{n=0}^{\infty} the sequence of monic Bergman orthogonal polynomials with respect to area measure on GG. Write γk\gamma_{k} for the normalizing constant of tkt_{k} (here we do not consider the weighted case of Bergman polynomials).

For pp a polynomial of degree nn we have by the orthogonality of the monomials

∫r​𝕋|p⁡(z)|2​d​|z|≤2​(n+1)r2​∫r​𝔻|p⁡(z)|2​𝑑A​(z).\int_{r{\mathbb{T}}}|p(z)|^{2}\mathrm{d}|z|\leq\frac{2(n+1)}{r^{2}}\int_{r{\mathbb{D}}}|p(z)|^{2}\mathrm{d}A(z).

Recall that βk2\beta_{k}^{2} minimizes ∫Γ|pk|2​d​|z|\int_{\Gamma}|p_{k}|^{2}\mathrm{d}|z| for monic polynomials, and γk2\gamma_{k}^{2} minimizes ∫G|pk|2​𝑑A​(z)\int_{G}|p_{k}|^{2}\mathrm{d}A(z). Therefore, we have

γn2=∫𝔻1|tn​(z)|2​𝑑A​(z)+∫𝔻2|tn​(z)|2​𝑑A​(z)≥f3​(η)n+1​∫Γ|tn​(z)|2​d​|z|≥f3​(η)n+1​βn2,\gamma_{n}^{2}=\int_{{\mathbb{D}}_{1}}|t_{n}(z)|^{2}\mathrm{d}A(z)+\int_{{\mathbb{D}}_{2}}|t_{n}(z)|^{2}\mathrm{d}A(z)\geq\frac{f_{3}(\eta)}{n+1}\int_{{\Gamma}}|t_{n}(z)|^{2}\mathrm{d}|z|\geq\frac{f_{3}(\eta)}{n+1}\beta_{n}^{2},

where f3f_{3} is some positive continuous function in η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1).

Using Theorem 4.18, we conclude the lower bound in Theorem 4.19

γn≥C1⋅Cap⁡(Γ)n+1n+1.\gamma_{n}\geq C_{1}\cdot\frac{\LCap\left({{\Gamma}}\right)^{n+1}}{\sqrt{n+1}}.

To prove the upper bound for γn\gamma_{n} we will use the following (very special case of) [Wid69, Thms. 8.38.3 and 5.65.6], concerning Chebyshev polynomials.

Theorem B.1.

Let Γ=∂G=𝕋1∪𝕋2{\Gamma}=\partial G={\mathbb{T}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{T}}_{2} be the boundary of the disks, as in Theorem 4.19. There is a constant MM depending continuously on the Green function 𝔤\mathfrak{g} of Γ{\Gamma} (w.r.t. ∞\infty) and its derivatives, such that for each nn, there is a monic polynomial QQ of degree nn satisfying

log⁡|Q⁡(z)|≤M+n​log⁡Cap⁡(Γ),∀z∈Γ.\log|Q(z)|\leq M+n\log\LCap\left({{\Gamma}}\right),\qquad\forall z\in{\Gamma}.
Remark.

By the assumptions MM can be bounded (continuously) in terms of η\eta.

Now we repeat the proof of [Gus+09, Lemma 8.2] in a simplified form. Let 𝔤=𝔤Ω\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{g}_{\Omega} be the Green function (always w.r.t. ∞\infty) for

Ω≔Gc=ℂ∖(𝔻1∪𝔻2).\Omega\coloneqq G^{c}={\mathbb{C}}\setminus({\mathbb{D}}_{1}\cup{\mathbb{D}}_{2}).

The function 𝔤\mathfrak{g} can be extended harmonically into the Green function (up to a constant) of a larger domain Ωτ\Omega_{\tau} which corresponds to the level set 𝔤=log⁡τ\mathfrak{g}=\log\tau with τ∈(0,1)\tau\in(0,1). This τ\tau may be chosen to be a continuous function of η\eta. Moreover, fixing some ρ=ρη∈(τ,1)\rho=\rho_{\eta}\in(\tau,1) in a continuous way in η\eta, we have for R≥ρR\geq\rho

𝔤R(z)≔𝔤ΩR(z)=𝔤(z)−logR,ΩR≔{𝔤≥logR}.\mathfrak{g}_{R}(z)\coloneqq\mathfrak{g}_{\Omega_{R}}(z)=\mathfrak{g}(z)-\log R,\qquad\Omega_{R}\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{g}\geq\log R\}.

Thus Cap⁡(∂ΩR)=R​Cap⁡(∂G)=R​Cap⁡(Γ)\LCap\left({\partial\Omega_{R}}\right)=R\LCap\left({\partial G}\right)=R\LCap\left({{\Gamma}}\right). By Theorem B.1 applied to ∂Ωρ\partial\Omega_{\rho} we have a polynomial QQ of degree nn such that

log⁡|Q⁡(z)|≤M+n​log⁡Cap⁡(∂Ωρ),∀z∈∂Ωρ,\log|Q(z)|\leq M+n\log\LCap\left({\partial\Omega_{\rho}}\right),\qquad\forall z\in\partial\Omega_{\rho},

where MM depends continuously on η\eta. By the maximum principle (for the unbounded domain Ωρ\Omega_{\rho}) this inequality extends to

log⁡|Q⁡(z)|≤M+n⁡(log⁡Cap⁡(∂Ωρ)+𝔤ρ​(z)),∀z∈Ωρ.\log|Q(z)|\leq M+n(\log\LCap\left({\partial\Omega_{\rho}}\right)+\mathfrak{g}_{\rho}(z)),\qquad\forall z\in\Omega_{\rho}.

Since 𝔤R​(z)+log⁡Cap⁡(∂ΩR)=log⁡Cap⁡(Γ)\mathfrak{g}_{R}(z)+\log\LCap\left({\partial\Omega_{R}}\right)=\log\LCap\left({{\Gamma}}\right) does not depend on RR, we have for R≥ρR\geq\rho

log⁡|Q⁡(z)|≤M+n​log​Cap⁡(∂ΩR)⟹|Q⁡(z)|≤M′​Rn​Cap​(Γ)n,∀z∈∂ΩR.\log|Q(z)|\leq M+n\log\LCap\left({\partial\Omega_{R}}\right)\implies|Q(z)|\leq M^{\prime}R^{n}\LCap\left({\Gamma}\right)^{n},\qquad\forall z\in\partial\Omega_{R}.

Now, by the usual maximum principle

(9) |Q⁡(z)|≤M′​Rn​Cap⁡(Γ)n,z∈ΩRc,ρ≤R<∞.|Q(z)|\leq M^{\prime}R^{n}\LCap\left({\Gamma}\right)^{n},\qquad z\in\Omega_{R}^{c},\>\rho\leq R<\infty.

We proceed to bound the L2​(G)L^{2}(G)-norm of QQ as in [Gus+09] by splitting GG into Ωρc\Omega_{\rho}^{c} and the rest. We bound the first part using (9). The integral over G∖ΩρG\setminus\Omega_{\rho} is bounded by foliating it by the level sets of ∂ΩR\partial\Omega_{R} using (9) and the coarea formula. For the convenience of the reader we provide the details below.

Write the integral over GG as follows

∫G|Q|2​𝑑A=∫Ωρc|Q|2​𝑑A+∫G∩Ωρ|Q|2​𝑑A≕I1+I2.\int_{G}|Q|^{2}\mathrm{d}A=\int_{\Omega_{\rho}^{c}}|Q|^{2}\mathrm{d}A+\int_{G\cap\Omega_{\rho}}|Q|^{2}\mathrm{d}A\eqqcolon I_{1}+I_{2}.

so that
